papers.title: FUSEMOS: Perceptual Evaluation of Text-to-Music Generation with Dual-Encoder Fusion and Ranking-Aware Composite Loss
papers.abstract: Perceptual evaluation of generated music is essential for developing text-to-music (TTM) generation systems. Existing automatic music perceptual evaluation methods rely solely on the contrastive language audio pretraining (CLAP) model to extract both audio and text features for predicting human-annotated mean opinion scores (MOS), particularly for overall musical impression (OMI) and textual alignment (TA). However, CLAP is limited in capturing fine-grained musical attributes such as timbre and expressiveness \emph{etc}. To address this, we propose FUSEMOS, a dual-encoder fusion framework that integrates CLAP with MERT, a self-supervised model pretrained on large scale music audio, to better capture both high level semantic alignment and detailed musical characteristics for more accurate OMI and TA estimation. Furthermore, to overcome the limitations of conventional regression losses in measuring human preferred relative ranking of music segments, we design a novel ranking-aware composite loss function. Experiments conducted on the MusicEval benchmark demonstrate that our approach outperforms the existing SOTA methods in both mean squared error and rank correlation metrics by a large margin.
reasons: Generative Music & Audio: text-to-music, music generation

papers.title: Route-DMD: Distribution Matching Distillation with Task-Routed Mechanism for Speech Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Speech foundation models built on flow matching handle generation, editing, and processing in one system, but every request costs 20-50 iterative steps, and classifier-free guidance (CFG) doubles each of them. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) trains a student that approaches the teacher's quality in a few steps, yet existing speech distillation work applies it to generation alone. We show that a distribution-matching objective does not serve every task: in separation, the noised states of erroneous student outputs deviate far from the teacher's training distribution, where its prediction is unreliable. Route-DMD therefore makes the objective task-dependent, routing the affected tasks to a regression loss and keeping decoupled distribution matching elsewhere. The student is initialized by consistency distillation, and teacher rollouts use adaptive projected guidance (APG) instead of CFG. Without CFG, the 4-step student matches the 32-step teacher on generation, editing, and processing tasks at a 4.5$\times$ end-to-end speedup.

papers.title: Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Chunk-Interleaved Full-Duplex Speech Language Models
papers.abstract: Chunk-interleaved full-duplex speech language models listen and speak in fixed time chunks, and each chunk must be processed before the next one arrives. Their workload is asymmetric across chunks: listen chunks leave compute idle while awaiting audio, and speak and tool-call chunks require serial generation, which delays responses and tool calls. Using the idle compute for the next chunk requires decoding it before its audio arrives, under an assumed input. Taking silence as the assumed input and comparing the output with the output under real audio on four models, we observe two properties. First, the next audio chunk does not change the output in 95.3% of chunks. Second, 88% of changes begin at the first output token. Building on these properties, we propose Speculative Listening, a training-free, lossless framework for input-time self-speculative decoding. During idle time, the model drafts the next chunk under silence and, for changes at the first token, a second branch from the runner-up first token. It keeps all drafts in a cross-chunk hypothesis pool and verifies them when the audio arrives. On our eight-task benchmark TickTock-Bench, Speculative Listening speeds up speak chunks by 2.6-2.8x and tool-call chunks by up to 23.4x. On average, it reduces the decoding delay before a response starts by 73%, to 74-241 ms, close to the 200 ms gap between human turns, and the maximum lag behind real time by 94.4%.

papers.title: Perlindungan Hukum Pemilik Suara Atas Voice Cloning Berbasis Artificial Intelligence tanpa Persetujuan
papers.abstract: Teknologi voice cloning berbasis kecerdasan artifisial kini membuat siapa saja bisa meniru suara orang lain tanpa meminta izin, padahal hukum Indonesia belum memperlakukan identitas vokal sebagai objek perlindungan yang berdiri sendiri. Artikel ini menelaah di mana sebenarnya kedudukan identitas vokal dalam hukum positif Indonesia dan perlindungan apa yang dapat diandalkan pemilik suara bila dilihat dari kacamata right of publicity. Metode yang dipakai adalah penelitian hukum normatif dengan pendekatan perundang-undangan, konseptual, dan perbandingan. Bahan hukum primer, sekunder, dan tersier dikumpulkan lewat studi kepustakaan, lalu dibaca secara kualitatif dengan penafsiran gramatikal, sistematis, dan teleologis. Hasilnya menunjukkan bahwa identitas vokal berada dalam posisi yang terpecah-pecah: hak cipta dan hak terkait hanya menjangkau ciptaan yang terfiksasi dan pertunjukan yang benar-benar terjadi, UU Pelindungan Data Pribadi memandang suara sebagai data pribadi terutama saat diolah untuk mengenali seseorang, dan belum ada satu instrumen pun yang mengakui nilai komersial suara yang dapat dikenali publik. Jika dibaca melalui pilar persetujuan, kompensasi, dan kendali dalam right of publicity, perlindungan masih bisa dirangkai, yakni secara preventif lewat lisensi yang spesifik dan pelabelan konten sintetis, serta secara represif lewat gugatan perbuatan melawan hukum, sanksi pelindungan data dan informasi elektronik, norma perlindungan konsumen, dan mekanisme penurunan konten. Artikel ini merekomendasikan norma sui generis yang mengakui identitas vokal sebagai hak kepribadian yang bernilai ekonomi.

papers.title: From Anti-Spoofing to Trustworthy Audio Forensics: A Bibliometric and Science-Mapping Review of Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: This study maps the intellectual structure, knowledge base, and emerging frontiers of audio-deepfake detection, addressing the absence of an integrated account of the field’s evolution, influence, collaboration, and thematic change. Metadata-based review bibliometric and science mapping analysis on 945 deduplicated Scopus and Web of Science articles(2020-2026) obtained on 23 July 2026, without any full text screening. Performance analysis, citation and co-citation analysis, bibliographic coupling, collaboration mapping, keyword co-occurrence, thematic mapping, and trend analysis were conducted using bibliometrix/Biblioshiny. The field expanded rapidly (56.9% complete-year annual growth) but remains conference-dominated and only selectively internationalised. ASVspoof and a small set of benchmark-centred studies form the intellectual core, while recent research is shifting towards self-supervised learning, cross-dataset generalisation, real-time detection, source tracing, and explainable forensics. Persistent gaps concern multilingual and low-resource data, robustness to unseen generators and channels, privacy, fairness, and operational validation. Keyword trends indicate increasing focus on auditability, provenance and deployable detection. Progress depends on standardised cross-language evaluation, representative real-world datasets, transparent uncertainty reporting, and closer integration of technical, ethical, and governance perspectives. The findings are limited by database, searches, keyword, and lack of full indexing for 2026.

papers.title: VoxCanvas-41M: A Large-Scale Bilingual Dataset for Instruction-Based Speech Editing and Its Learning Dynamics
papers.abstract: Recent advances in speech generation have spurred the development of speech editing techniques. However, achieving high-quality speech editing remains challenging due to two key limitations. First, the major hurdle is the lack of large-scale, high-quality speech editing datasets. Constructing such datasets is costly, while open-source, scalable data pipelines remain limited. Second, the learning dynamics of speech editing models remain poorly understood. In particular, how models acquire editing capabilities and the relationship between generation and editing remain unclear. To address these challenges, we introduce VoxCanvas-41M, a large-scale bilingual dataset comprising approximately 41 million speech editing pairs. VoxCanvas-41M covers two major categories: content editing, including single-span, multi-span, and location-reference editing, and paralinguistic editing, covering the insertion and deletion of 39 classes of nonverbal events such as laughter, sighs, and coughs. Building on VoxCanvas-41M, we train VoxCanvas-Edit, an instruction-based speech editing model, demonstrating the effectiveness of our dataset in improving editing performance. Furthermore, we systematically investigate the learning dynamics of speech editing, examining how models learn different editing operations and how data scale, task interactions, and training strategies affect editing performance. The dataset, pipeline, and demos are publicly available.

--- language: - en license: apache-2.0 base_model: FunAudioLLM/Fun-Audio-Chat-8B pipeline_tag: audio-to-audio tags: - full-duplex - speech-to-speech - spoken-dialogue - audio-language-model --- # Awaken Full Duplex
**Awaken: Efficient Full-Duplex Adaptation with Capability Retention** [![Project Page](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blog-Project%20Page-orange)](https://avera-labs.github.io/AwakenFullDuplex/) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Code-blue)](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex) [![Hugging Face](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97-Model-yellow)](https://huggingface.co/openmartdev/awaken-full-duplex) [![Base model](https://img.shields.io/badge/Base-Fun--Audio--Chat--8B-green)](https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/Fun-Audio-Chat-8B)
## Model Description Full-duplex voice models can listen and speak at the same time, so they can acknowledge, interrupt, and hand over turns the way people do. Teaching this usually depends on natural conversational audio rich in backchannels. That audio is scarce, and without careful curation it can weaken a model's reasoning and grounding. **Awaken** learns full-duplex behavior from a small amount of such data and keeps its base model's scores.

### Key Features - **Efficient**: Starts from the half-duplex [Fun-Audio-Chat-8B](https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/Fun-Audio-Chat-8B) checkpoint and teaches turn-taking with composed conversations that have explicit timing, overlap, and interruptions. Two supervised stages and a short reinforcement-learning stage are enough; there is no large-scale duplex pretraining. - **Effective**: A targeted GRPO stage raises the backchannel pass rate from 1% (supervised training alone) to **63%**, while taking the floor in only **3%** of items. - **Retains model ability**: Passes **61%** of groundedness probes, near its half-duplex base (66%) and well above open full-duplex models (14–35%). Solves **90%** of spoken logic puzzles, compared with 30–40% for open full-duplex models.

### Training Recipe

1. **Stage 1 SFT**: learns the streaming input pattern and aligned text and speech targets on 64,000 composed conversations (windows up to 180 s). 2. **Stage 2 SFT**: blends the stage-1 weights 50/50 with the base checkpoint, then continues on 100,132 records with replay of the interaction data. 3. **GRPO**: improves backchannel timing from the model's own samples in conversational windows. See the [project page](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex/blob/main/webpage/index.html) for the full data composition and training details. ## Model Details | Attribute | Value | |-----------|-------| | Model Size | ~8B parameters | | Base Model | [Fun-Audio-Chat-8B](https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/Fun-Audio-Chat-8B) (half-duplex) | | Backbone | Qwen3-8B, one position per 200 ms frame | | Input | Streaming 24 kHz user audio through a causal Whisper-style encoder (2 s attention window) | | Output | Text tokens and 5 codec tokens per frame, rendered by the CosyVoice3 flow decoder and HiFT vocoder | | Interaction | Full-duplex: no turns, no voice-activity detector | | Languages | English | | License | Apache 2.0 (same as the base model) | ## Requirements - Linux with an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) - Python >= 3.10 - PyTorch >= 2.7 (tested with 2.8, CUDA 12.8) - TensorRT 10 ## Installation ```bash git clone https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex cd AwakenFullDuplex # 1. torch + torchaudio for YOUR CUDA driver first (the default PyPI wheel targets the newest # CUDA and will not load on older drivers), e.g. for CUDA 12.8: pip install torch torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 # 2. the package pip install -e . # Linux + CUDA GPU; pulls transformers, tensorrt, ... pip install -e ".[fast]" # + flash-attn (faster decode; optional) pip install -e ".[voice]" # + onnxruntime, to make voice prompts from a clip ``` ## Quick Start ### Download Models ```bash pip install huggingface-hub hf download openmartdev/awaken-full-duplex --local-dir ./pretrained_models/awaken-chat ``` The speech codec is fetched automatically from [`FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512`](https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512) (flow, vocoder and the estimator's ONNX export only). The TensorRT engine is built once per machine on first use, which takes a few minutes. ### Inference Live server (one conversation at a time, WebSocket protocol in `awaken_chat/server/protocol.py`): ```bash awaken-server --model ./pretrained_models/awaken-chat --port 8998 [--ssl-dir certs] [--voices-dir assets/voices] ``` Offline, with a recorded user track: ```bash awaken-offline --model ./pretrained_models/awaken-chat --input user.wav --out out/ # stereo.wav, transcript.txt, tokens.pt ``` Make a voice prompt from a reference clip (3-10 s of one speaker you have the rights to): ```bash awaken-voice --clip speaker.wav --out assets/voices/speaker.pt ``` From Python: ```python from awaken_chat import load_model, Decoders, DuplexSession, system_prompt loaded = load_model("./pretrained_models/awaken-chat") # HF repo id or local directory decoders = Decoders(loaded.model) # static caches + CUDA graphs, once per process session = DuplexSession(loaded.model, decoders, loaded.prompt_ids(system_prompt("You are a tour guide."))) for features in ear_frames: # (5, 4096) per 200 ms, see models/ear.py out = session.step(features) # out.text_id, out.audio_ids, out.state ``` ## Evaluation We measure listener behavior, following the conversation, and knowledge and reasoning side by side. Awaken and Fun-Audio-Chat-8B are run by us; other rows come from the public InteractionBench results and the Fun-Audio-Chat technical report. | System | Backchannel pass ↑ | Floor-take ↓ | Groundedness probes ↑ | Logic puzzles ↑ | Llama Q. ↑ | TriviaQA ↑ | |--------|-------------------:|-------------:|----------------------:|----------------:|-----------:|-----------:| | GPT-Realtime | 10% | 5% | 67% | 100% | – | – | | Moshi | 78% | 22% | 14% | 30% | 65.67 | 18.46 | | Freeze-Omni | 0% | 39% | 35% | 40% | 74.00 | 30.08 | | PersonaPlex | 83% | 11% | 30% | 30% | – | – | | Fun-Audio-Chat-Duplex-8B | – | – | – | – | 72.33 | 29.59 | | Fun-Audio-Chat-8B (half-duplex base) | n/a | n/a | 66% | 100% | 76.2 | 48.7 | | Awaken SFT | 1% | 6% | 62% | 87% | 70.7 | 35.5 | | **Awaken GRPO** | **63%** | **3%** | **61%** | **90%** | **73.4** | **36.2** | - **Backchannels**: 30 InteractionBench storytelling items × 3 seeds. An item passes when the assistant backchannels at least once and never takes the floor. A half-duplex model cannot speak while the user is speaking, so the base model is n/a. - **Groundedness**: 10 conversations of 22–24 turns, then 52 probes (recall, updates, unknown information, constraints, false premises, nonsense questions). Our rows are means over 5–30 runs judged on the model's text stream; published rows judge transcripts of the audio. - **Logic puzzles**: 10 InteractionBench puzzles × 3 seeds, judged on the model's text stream. - **Spoken QA**: our rows are means over 3 seeds; Freeze-Omni, Moshi and Fun-Audio-Chat-Duplex-8B are reported scores from Table 7 of the Fun-Audio-Chat technical report. | System | OpenBookQA ↑ | |--------|-------------:| | Fun-Audio-Chat-8B (half-duplex) | 83.52 | | Fun-Audio-Chat-Duplex-8B (reported) | – | | Freeze-Omni (reported) | 30.98 | | Moshi (reported) | 25.93 | | Awaken SFT | 76.2 | | **Awaken GRPO** | **75.6** | Because our runs and the published results are scored differently, compare across systems with care. Full methodology is on the [project page](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex/blob/main/webpage/index.html). ## Inference Details
How the inference stack works Every 200 ms ("one frame") the model consumes * the user's audio of that frame, through a causal **ear** (a Whisper-style encoder with a 2 s attention window), * its own previous frame: one **text token** and five **codec tokens** of its own voice, and predicts the next text token and the next five codec tokens. The text lane carries the words and two control tokens: `pad` means "listening" and, during speech, "I am done" (the release); `sil` means "words done, audio still finishing". The codec tokens are rendered to speech by CosyVoice3's flow-matching decoder and HiFT vocoder. ``` mic 24 kHz ─► StreamingEar ─► 5 feature vectors per frame ─┐ ▼ own text token ──► Qwen3-8B backbone (one position per frame) ──► next text token own codec tokens ─┘ │ ▼ depth decoder (5 codec tokens / frame) ──► CosyVoice3 flow + HiFT ──► speaker ``` Both transformer stacks run through a fused, CUDA-graphed single-token decoder with static key/value caches (`awaken_chat/inference/static_decoder.py`), so a frame costs a few milliseconds of launch overhead instead of thousands of small kernels.
Decode parameters `DecodeParams` (`awaken_chat/inference/params.py`) has two presets. `bench` is the recipe the reported numbers were produced with (text T 0.7 / top-k 25, audio T 0.8 / top-k 250). `live` is sharper inside a text burst (T 0.2 / top-k 5), penalizes repeated content tokens and caps consecutive near-silent codec tokens; it is what the server uses by default. Any field can be overridden per conversation in the `start` message.
Repository layout ``` awaken_chat/ frame.py frame rate, group size, sample rates, special token ids, system prompt models/ configuration, ear, token embedder, depth decoder, AwakenModel, loaders inference/ static decoder, session state machine, sampling, decode params, offline runner codec/ CosyVoice3 flow + HiFT (vendored, trimmed), streaming detokenizer, worker process, voices server/ WebSocket protocol, live session runner, FastAPI app cli.py awaken-server / awaken-offline / awaken-voice scripts/ ws_client.py, a paced WebSocket client that drives the server from a wav file tests/ CPU unit tests on tiny random models hf_model_card/ Hugging Face model card (README + figures) webpage/ project page ```
## License The code and model weights are licensed under the [Apache 2.0 License](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex/blob/main/LICENSE), the same license as the base model [Fun-Audio-Chat-8B](https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/Fun-Audio-Chat-8B). ## Acknowledgments The model architecture is derived from [Fun-Audio-Chat](https://github.com/FunAudioLLM/Fun-Audio-Chat) and the speech codec from [CosyVoice](https://github.com/FunAudioLLM/CosyVoice) (both Apache-2.0); the text backbone is [Qwen3](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3), and the ear follows [Whisper](https://github.com/openai/whisper)'s encoder. See [`NOTICE`](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex/blob/main/NOTICE). ## Contact - 🐛 Submit an [Issue](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex/issues) - 💡 Submit a [Pull Request](https://github.com/avera-labs/AwakenFullDuplex/pulls)

# StaleyNET checkpoints

[![Source on GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/source-GitHub-1D1B20?logo=github)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet) [![staleynet-audio on crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/staleynet-audio?label=staleynet-audio)](https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio) [![Paper](https://img.shields.io/badge/paper-PDF-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/blob/main/paper/preprint.pdf) [![Book](https://img.shields.io/badge/book-mdBook-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/tree/main/book/src) [![Release v0.1.2](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/arpanpathak/staleynet)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases) [![Dataset: 3.1 GB](https://img.shields.io/badge/dataset-3.1%20GB-FFD21E?logo=huggingface&logoColor=black)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/arpanpathak/staleynet-data)

Weights for **StaleyNET**, a text-prompted music generator trained from random initialization in Rust on NVIDIA edge GPUs. The Transformer, residual vector quantizer, Griffin-Lim vocoder, and GPU kernels are implemented in the project.

The code, paper, and book live in the companion repository:
<https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet>.

## Release v0.1.2

- GitHub release: <https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases/tag/v0.1.2>
- `staleynet-audio` 0.1.2 on crates.io: <https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio>. Its page explains each audio step with intuition and runnable examples.
- Since v0.1.1: the GPU kernels are organised into one module per topic, the AGX Thor builds against cuda-oxide's main branch, and the paper has been revised with hardware, benchmark and tokenizer appendices.
- New in these repositories: the `lyrics-thor`, `lyrics-thor-long` and `pq-large` runs, and the band-group token caches they train on.
- CI: rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, cargo-deny, the audio coverage gate, and documentation tests for every example on the crate page.

## At a glance

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Checkpointed runs | 9 |
| Parameters | 7,099,904 for text-only runs; 7,165,440 for the lyrics runs; 42,858,496 for `pq-large` |
| Transformer | width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, context 768 (`pq-large`: width 512, 8 layers, context 1152) |
| Audio tokens | 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries (`pq-large`: 4 band groups × 4 levels = 16 codebooks of 1024 entries) |
| Audio features | 128 mel bands at 24 kHz, FFT 1024, hop 256 |
| Training data | Song Describer Dataset and JamendoLyrics MultiLang |
| License | CC BY-SA 4.0, subject to the upstream dataset terms |

## Checkpoints

| Run | Purpose | Parameters | `best` step | `latest` step | Training tracks |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `thor-base` | base text-to-music model | 7,099,904 | 0 | None | 667 |
| `smoke` | pipeline smoke test | 7,099,904 | 0 | 1,500 | 667 |
| `overfit-one-take` | single-take memorisation check | 7,099,904 | 200 | 200 | 1 |
| `vocal-scratch` | vocal-filtered model from scratch | 7,099,904 | 5,500 | 6,000 | 281 |
| `vocal-finetune` | vocal fine-tune | 7,099,904 | 250 | None | 281 |
| `lyrics-orin` | lyrics-conditioned model | 7,165,440 | 3,750 | 4,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor` | lyrics-conditioned model trained on the AGX Thor | 7,165,440 | 4,750 | 8,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor-long` | the same model trained for 20,000 steps | 7,165,440 | 19,750 | 20,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `pq-large` | larger model on the band-group tokenizer (in progress) | 42,858,496 | 7,000 | 7,000 | 742 (75 with lyrics) |

The step values are exactly what each `model.json` records. `best/` is the weight-only checkpoint selected by validation. `latest/` is the resumable checkpoint with AdamW moments. Some early runs stored only `best/`, and `thor-base` and `smoke` record step 0 in their `best/model.json`. Where a `latest/` exists, prefer it for the late training state.

### About `pq-large`

`pq-large` is still training on the Jetson AGX Thor (128 GB). The files here are a snapshot at step 7,000 of 20,000, and they will be replaced as the run advances. Its validation loss (5.135 nats per token at step 7,000) is averaged over 16 codebooks of a different tokenizer, so it cannot be compared directly with the 4-codebook runs above.

The model reads codes from the band-group tokenizer, which splits the 128 mel bands into 4 groups and quantises each group with 4 residual levels. That tokenizer is stored as `checkpoints/pq-large/tokenizer.json`, and the matching caches are `cache-g4l4f1/`, `cache-pq-jamendolyrics/` and `cache-pq-recordings/` in the dataset repository. Pass `--cache data/cache-g4l4f1` when generating with this run.

`evaluations/<run>/` holds the paired lyrics test of each lyrics run: the per-track loss with aligned, removed and mismatched lyrics.

## Training progress

The runs on the Jetson AGX Thor publish their metrics here every two hours
(`deploy/hf/publish.sh` in the code repository): `metrics/<run>.jsonl` holds
every logged event, and `plots/<run>.png` shows, from left to right, the
training and validation loss in nats per code against optimizer step, the
latest validation loss of each codebook (coarse levels are far easier to
predict than fine ones), and the throughput in positions per second.

![pq-large training curves](plots/pq-large.png)

## Layout

```text
checkpoints/<run>/best/      weights only       model.json + tensors.bin
checkpoints/<run>/latest/    weights + AdamW    model.json + tensors.bin
configs/                     canonical training configurations
run-configs/                 per-run config.json where the run saved one
metrics/                     full metrics.jsonl for every run
logs/                        captured training logs and the tokenizer sweeps
evaluations/<run>/           paired lyrics evaluations
```

`tensors.bin` is little-endian `f32` in parameter-visitor order. `latest/` appends the AdamW first moments and then the second moments. `model.json` records the tensor manifest, the step, whether optimizer state is present, and the training configuration.

## Download and use

```bash
hf download arpanpathak/staleynet-checkpoints \
  --repo-type model --local-dir staleynet-checkpoints

# From the code repository, on a Jetson with the cuda-oxide toolchain:
cargo oxide build -- --release
staleynet sing \
  --cache data/cache \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/thor-base/best \
  --prompt "slow acoustic ballad, warm female voice" \
  --out song.wav
```

For the lyrics model:

```bash
staleynet sing \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/lyrics-orin/best \
  --prompt "grunge rock, raw male voice" \
  --lyrics-file song.txt \
  --out song.wav
```

Architecture: width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, feed-forward multiplier 4, context length 768, 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries, 128 mel bands at 24 kHz. `lyrics-orin` adds a 256-byte lyrics field.

## Training data and licensing

- **Song Describer Dataset** (SDD), Zenodo record [10072001](https://zenodo.org/records/10072001): 706 Jamendo recordings with human captions. Captions are CC BY-SA 4.0. The recordings carry the per-track Creative Commons licenses in `audio_licenses.txt`, including CC BY-NC-ND and CC BY-NC-SA.
- **JamendoLyrics MultiLang**, <https://github.com/f90/jamendolyrics>: code and metadata are MIT. Songs and lyrics carry the per-song CC licenses in `JamendoLyrics.csv`.

Because the training audio includes NonCommercial and NoDerivatives tracks, these checkpoints are research artifacts, not a commercial product. Do not use them commercially where the upstream recording licenses forbid it, and do not use them to impersonate a singer without consent.

# Matoub-4B

A 4B-parameter text-to-speech model for **Kabyle** (Taqbaylit, `kab`, Latin script), trained on 384,960 curated speech pairs from Common Voice Kabyle. It synthesises broadcast-quality **24 kHz audio** from Kabyle text. Voice cloning is a feature of that model: a short reference recording, with its transcript kept in the original language, sets the speaker.

The reference can be Kabyle or another language. `generate()` produces one utterance at the trained adapter scale, for every reference language. An 8-codebook discrete audio representation carries Kabyle's phonology, including spirantised, pharyngealised, emphatic, and geminated consonants.

## Results

Validation was conducted across 16 utterances spanning six speakers. Each utterance was generated once with the packaged sampler. Speaker similarity is the cosine of WavLM embeddings (`microsoft/wavlm-base-plus-sv`), and transcription fidelity is measured with Fadhma-300M.

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| utterances | 16 |
| terminated | 15 / 16 |
| **mean voice cosine** | **0.881** |
| CER excess over real-audio floor | 0.045 |

The measured mean voice cosine of 0.881 confirms consistent speaker identity retention
across reference speakers. The CER excess measures character error rate relative to human
recordings of the same texts.

## Intended use

- **Kabyle audio production**: narration, dialogue, and spoken content.
- **Accessibility**: screen readers and voice interfaces for Kabyle speakers.
- **Language learning**: pronunciation material and spoken references.
- **Voice research**: cross-lingual speech synthesis and reference conditioning.

**Not suitable for**: biometric identification, impersonation, or safety-critical applications.

## Usage

```bash
pip install "transformers==5.17.0" "torch==2.11.0" "torchaudio==2.11.0" soundfile onnxruntime
```

Load the model with `transformers`. The custom architecture is loaded directly via
`trust_remote_code=True`:

```python
import soundfile as sf
from transformers import AutoModelForTextToWaveform

REPO = "agbalu/Matoub-4B"
model = AutoModelForTextToWaveform.from_pretrained(REPO, trust_remote_code=True).to("cuda").eval()

speech = model.generate(
    text="Azul fell-awen! Ass-a ad nemmeslay s teqbaylit.",
    reference_audio="voice.wav",
    reference_text="The exact words spoken in voice.wav, in their original language.",
)

sf.write("speech.wav", speech.waveform[0].numpy(), speech.sampling_rate, subtype="FLOAT")
```

### Notes

- `text`: target Kabyle text to synthesise.
- `reference_audio`: path to clean reference audio of the target speaker.
- Use clear, continuous speech from one speaker, without background music, overlapping voices or heavy reverberation. No single optimal reference duration has been established for this release.
- `reference_text`: exact transcript of the words spoken in `reference_audio` in their original language.
- For an English or French reference, provide the exact English or French transcript; do not translate it into Kabyle.
- `generate()` writes one utterance. It does not search candidates or download an ASR or speaker verifier.
- A text that cannot fit in the 8,192-position context with its reference is split, then joined. Leading and trailing silence is removed, and an internal silence longer than 320 ms is shortened to 140 ms.
- The returned waveform is a CPU float tensor sampled at 24,000 Hz.
- Sampling, decoding and the adapter scale live in `model.config.inference`.

### Generation settings and return value

`.generate()` accepts `text`, `reference_audio`, `reference_text`, and optional
`output_path`. Sampling settings are configured before generation:

```python
model.config.inference["sampling"].update(
    temperature=0.8,
    top_p=0.8,
    top_k=30,
    max_new_positions=1500,
)
```

These are the packaged sampling defaults. `max_new_positions` limits generated codec positions; it is not a waveform sample count. The return value is `SpeechOutput`:

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| `.waveform` | CPU float tensor with shape `[1, N]` |
| `.sampling_rate` | `24000` |
| `.report` | Generation audit: duration, checksum, sampler, and one trace per segment |

The audit records the sample that was produced. It does not select among several takes.

### 4-bit Quantization (NF4)

Install the additional quantization dependencies:

```bash
pip install "bitsandbytes==0.50.2" "accelerate==1.15.0"
```

For consumer GPUs and low-memory environments (e.g. RTX 3060, T4, 8 GB laptop GPUs), load the model using 4-bit NormalFloat (`nf4`). The transformer backbone is compressed while the neural vocoder automatically remains in high precision:

```python
import soundfile as sf
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForTextToWaveform, BitsAndBytesConfig

REPO = "agbalu/Matoub-4B"
bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)

model = AutoModelForTextToWaveform.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    quantization_config=bnb_config,
    device_map="auto",
    trust_remote_code=True,
).eval()

speech = model.generate(
    text="Azul fell-awen! Ass-a ad nemmeslay s teqbaylit.",
    reference_audio="voice.wav",
    reference_text="The exact words spoken in voice.wav, in their original language.",
)

sf.write("speech.wav", speech.waveform[0].numpy(), speech.sampling_rate, subtype="FLOAT")
```

The NF4 loading path was verified, including preservation of the audio codec in
FP32. On the measured single-candidate development panel, it reduced memory but
degraded pronunciation and completion relative to BF16. Prefer BF16 for the
Python quality baseline.

| Loading format | Measured peak device memory (decimal GB) |
|---|---:|
| BF16 | 9.94 |
| BitsAndBytes NF4 | 4.57 |

These peaks were measured on an H100 MIG using single-candidate decoding, with
quality scoring on CPU. They are not full-pipeline hardware requirements:
GPU-based verification models and longer contexts require additional memory.
Other GPU types were not benchmarked.

### Companion GGUF release

Standalone `q4_k`, `q8_0`, and `bf16` GGUF packages are prepared separately at
[`agbalu/Matoub-4B-GGUF`](https://huggingface.co/agbalu/Matoub-4B-GGUF).
See that card for runtime requirements, measurements and format-specific limits.

## Architecture

Matoub-4B couples an autoregressive multimodal transformer backbone with an 8-codebook 24 kHz neural audio codec. Parameter adaptation targets all projection pathways across every decoder layer, optimizing speech synthesis and phonetic fidelity while preserving the extensive cross-lingual acoustic representations of the foundation model.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Parameters** | **4,109,540,864** |
| Base model | bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b |
| Codec | bosonai/higgs-audio-v2-tokenizer (8 codebooks, 24 kHz) |
| Output | 24 kHz mono audio |
| Context length | Up to 8,192 positions |
| Interface | Transformers `AutoModelForTextToWaveform` (`trust_remote_code=True`) |

## Training data

Trained on Common Voice 26.0 Kabyle speech resampled to 24 kHz. Utterances are paired with
distinct same-speaker reference recordings sharing no text or audio overlap.

| split | pairs |
|---|---|
| train | 384,960 |
| validation | 29,812 |
| test | 5,871 |
| **total** | **420,643** |

## Training recipe

| | |
|---|---|
| Objective | Autoregressive cross-entropy over 8 codec streams |
| Adaptation | Rank-32 LoRA (alpha 64) |
| Optimizer | AdamW |
| Learning rate | 5e-5 with cosine decay to 5e-6 |
| Batch size | 32 |
| Precision | bfloat16 |
| Steps | 12,030 |
| Final loss | 3.8997 nats |

## Limitations

- **Pronunciation edge cases**: Proper nouns, loanwords, or atypical spellings outside the training corpus may require manual pronunciation adjustments.
- **Language specificity**: Optimized specifically for Kabyle (`kab`). Sibling Amazigh varieties (e.g. Tarifit, Tashelhit) have distinct phonological structures and are not covered.

## Files

| file | description |
|---|---|
| `model.safetensors` | Model weights, the rank-32 LoRA factors at the trained scale, and the audio codec |
| `config.json` | Model configuration and AutoClass mapping |
| `tokenizer.json`, `tokenizer_config.json`, `chat_template.jinja` | Text tokenizer and template |
| `modeling_speech.py` and supporting modules | Transformers model implementation |
| `requirements.txt` | Runtime dependencies |
| `export.stats.json` | Package checksums and metadata |
| `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` | Licensing terms |

## Reproduction

Trained on 384,960 Common Voice 26.0 Kabyle pairs for 12,030 steps from `bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b`. All reported metrics reproduce directly from the published weights and configuration.

## The name

**Lounès Matoub** (1956–1998) was one of the most celebrated Kabyle singers and poets of the 20th century, and an iconic advocate for Taqbaylit. Across 36 albums recorded in Kabyle, his music and poetry made the language vibrant and audible to generations of listeners.

His voice remains deeply tied to the preservation and cultural vitality of the language. Naming a Kabyle speech synthesis model after him is an homage to that legacy: using technology to make the language heard and spoken.

The naming is homage; it implies no affiliation or endorsement.

# KittenTTS 2

A 1.7B speech language model with in-context voice cloning. It reads text and writes S3
codec tokens, which a vocoder turns into 24 kHz audio.

```bash
pip install kittenml
```

```python
from kittenml import KittenTTS
import soundfile as sf

m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2")

# a built-in voice
audio = m.generate("Hi! umm.. how are you, I guess?  .. uh.. nice to meet you??",
                   voice="WeatherPresenterCheerful")

# or clone one, from 5-30 seconds of a single speaker
audio = m.generate("This is my own voice.", reference="my_voice.wav")

sf.write("output.wav", audio, m.sample_rate)
```

Everything the model needs is in this repository, so no Hugging Face login is required.

## Voices

`m.available_voices` lists all 115. Bella, Jasper, Luna, Bruno, Rosie, Hugo, Kiki
and Leo are the same speakers as in KittenTTS 0.8, so existing code keeps working.

Voices named after a person are English. The rest are named for the language they
speak followed by what they are — `SpanishAbuela`, `JapaneseTrainConductor`,
`RussianBabushka` — and are how you reach those languages, since the voice is what
carries the accent. Nine older entries carry a bare language name: Arabic, Chinese,
French, German, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish.

```python
m.generate("Guten Morgen. Ich wünsche dir einen wunderschönen Tag.",
           voice="German", normalize=False)

m.generate("Buenas tardes. Hoy vamos a preparar algo muy especial.",
           voice="SpanishAbuela", normalize=False)
```

Sixteen languages have a named voice: Arabic, Chinese, Dutch, French, German, Hindi,
Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Turkish,
and English.

Pass `normalize=False` for non-English text: the text normalizer is English-tuned and
will mangle numbers and dates in other languages.

## Expression controls

> **Beta.** Emotion control steers delivery rather than guaranteeing it, and the effect
> varies by voice and by sentence.

```python
m.generate("[joyful] We won the grant <laugh> I can (((hardly))) believe it!",
           voice="Kiki", preset="expressive")
```

A leading `[emotion]` tag, inline `<event>` tags and `(((emphasis)))` spans reach the
model as markup rather than being spoken, and switch on its expression conditioning.

**Emotions** — one leading tag sets the emotion for the whole line:

`[angry]` `[contemplative]` `[excited]` `[joyful]` `[mundane]`
`[nervous]` `[sad]` `[stern]` `[surprised]` `[tender]`

**Vocal events** — inline, anywhere in the line:

`<gasp>` `<giggle>` `<growl>` `<gulp>` `<laugh>`
`<pause>` `<scoff>` `<sigh>` `<sob>` `<um>`

**Emphasis** — triple parentheses stress a word or short phrase:

```python
m.generate("I told you (((never))) to open that door.", voice="Victor")
```

Only these twenty tags are recognised. They are the most common of the many in the
training data, so a rarer one such as `[reverent]` is spoken as ordinary text rather
than treated as markup — as is anything else bracketed, like `section [3]` or `x < 5`.

## Weight variants

The language model ships in three packings of the same weights. `weights=` picks one;
`model.available_weights` lists them.

| `weights=` | On disk | |
|---|---|---|
| `"packed"` *(default)* | 954 MB | 1.58-bit ternary body, bf16 embedding. **Lossless** |
| `"emb4"` | 469 MB | Same body in TL2, plus a 4-bit embedding. **Lossy** |
| `"full"` | 3469 MB | Plain bf16 |

```python
m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2", weights="emb4")
```

Only the variant you ask for is downloaded.

`emb4` halves the download, and the saving is almost entirely the token embedding — 324M
parameters that `packed` has to leave at bf16 because they are not ternary. Its transformer
body is still bit-exact: all 313 non-embedding tensors reproduce `full` exactly. The
embedding is not, at L2 relative error 0.118 against the bf16 export, and it is coded at
4.21 bits per weight across three frequency tiers. That is the one lossy thing here, which
is why `packed` stays the default.

## Decoders

Audio is decoded in two stages, and the first can be swapped for a smaller distilled
student with weights packed to 4 or 8 bits:

```python
m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2", decoder="student_w4")
```

| Decoder | Flow on disk | |
|---|---|---|
| `default` | 459 MB | Best quality |
| `student_w4` | 39 MB | Distilled single-step student, weights packed to 4 bits |

These trade fidelity for footprint, not for speed: quantisation shrinks storage and
memory bandwidth, not arithmetic.

## What is in here

```
lm/          the speech language model, plus its spk_proj speaker head
speaker/     the speaker-embedding model used when cloning
voices/      reference clips, transcripts, and precomputed embeddings
decoders/    the optional 4-bit decoder
cpp/         GGUF weights for the llama.cpp fork, see "Running on CPU"
config.json  token layout, decode presets, voice and decoder indexes
```

The weights are 947 MiB: 910 MiB for the language model and 37 MiB for the decoder.
A load pulls those rather than the whole repository, and only the decoder you ask for.

The language model's linear weights are ternary — within every 128-wide group each
value is exactly one of `{-scale, 0, +scale}` — so bf16 spends 16 bits to say one of
three things. `lm/model-ternary.safetensors` packs them five trits to a byte, 1.6 bits
per weight, with each group keeping its scale at full precision:

| | |
|---|---|
| `lm/model.safetensors` | 3.47 GB, bf16 throughout |
| `lm/model-ternary.safetensors` | **0.95 GB**, the same weights, 3.6x smaller |

The packing is exact rather than approximate, so the two produce bit-identical audio.
`config.json` points `lm_packed` at the smaller file and that is what gets downloaded;
the full file stays for anything loading this with plain `transformers`.

## Running on CPU

KittenTTS 2 runs on CPU out of the box — `device` is auto-detected — but the fastest way
is [kitten-tts-2-cpp](https://github.com/KittenML/kitten-tts-2-cpp), our llama.cpp fork.
The `cpp/` directory here holds what it needs: the GGUF language model and its decoders.

## Requirements

Python 3.10 or later, and PyTorch.

## License

These weights are released under the [Stellon Labs Community License](LICENSE.md). Research,
non-commercial and limited commercial use are free of charge; the commercial grant ends once you
or your affiliates pass USD $1,000,000 in annual revenue or in total cumulative funding, at which
point you need a separate license from Stellon Labs. Distributing the weights, a derivative, or a
product built on them carries attribution requirements — see Section IV(a).

Two things in here are covered by their own terms instead: `speaker/`, the pyannote
speaker-embedding model, under [MIT](speaker/LICENSE), and the `kittenml` Python package that
loads this repository, under Apache 2.0.

# OGG TTS **Expressive multilingual text-to-speech with block diffusion**
> **Preview release.** This is checkpoint 120k of a 400k-step pre-training run that is still in progress, with a new > acoustic decoder (axial MTP). Updated checkpoints will be published as new revisions of this repository; the earlier > 20k and 40k previews (previous architecture) stay available in the history. ## Overview OGG TTS is a 0.75B-parameter zero-shot text-to-speech model trained on about 8,200 hours of studio-quality speech in English, Polish, Spanish, German, Russian, French, Portuguese and Italian. It generates discrete tokens of the Fish Audio 44.1 kHz codec with **block diffusion**: - each block of 0.74 s is produced in parallel by iterative unmasking; - blocks follow one another left to right, so audio can be streamed as soon as the first block is ready. The backbone is initialised from OmniVoice (Qwen3-0.6B, masked discrete diffusion). An axial multi-token prediction (MTP) decoder then fills in the acoustic detail of the block: the 9 residual codebooks, one per step, for all frames at once. The name comes from the trolls of *The Witcher*. OGG is the first of three architectures (OGG, ROGG, POGG) that we compare in an upcoming technical report. ### Highlights - **Expressive by default.** The model reads with natural, context-appropriate emotion. - **Optional inline tags.** 24 tags for emotion, delivery and vocal events, placed exactly where they should take effect. - **Zero-shot voice cloning.** From a few seconds of reference audio, or one of the built-in speaker identities without any prompt. - **Context-aware delivery.** Neighbouring lines can be given as text context, so a line of dialogue or a sentence of a story fits its scene. - **Streaming.** Finished blocks never change and can be played immediately. ## Emotion and expression tags Tags are optional. Without them the model infers the delivery from the text and its context. With them it follows the requested emotion or sound at the given position: ```text [frustrated] Not again… [sighing] Fine, I'll do it myself. [scared] [whispering] Someone is here… [shouting] Run! They're right behind us! ``` | Group | Tags | |---|---| | Emotion | `[angry]` `[frustrated]` `[excited]` `[tired]` `[playful]` `[sad]` `[scared]` `[shouting]` | | Delivery | `[whispering]` `[softly]` `[voice breaking]` `[singing]` `[pause]` `[slowly]` | | Vocal events | `[laughing]` `[sighing]` `[gasping]` `[panting]` `[coughing]` `[clears throat]` `[sniffling]` `[scoffing]` `[yawning]` `[humming]` | The labels come from an audio-language-model pass over **502,668 sentences**, i.e. the audio with its transcript, under a closed list of 24 tags. The model was instructed to tag only what is audible in the recording, never what the text alone suggests. 57,016 sentences (11 %) received at least one tag; the rest carry a checked transcript without tags, so the model also learns when *not* to add an effect. Tags are dropped from part of the training samples, which keeps them optional at inference time. | Tag | Examples | Tag | Examples | Tag | Examples | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | `[shouting]` | 19,407 | `[laughing]` | 2,621 | `[tired]` | 708 | | `[angry]` | 10,287 | `[scared]` | 1,847 | `[slowly]` | 419 | | `[frustrated]` | 5,565 | `[whispering]` | 1,502 | `[clears throat]` | 356 | | `[pause]` | 4,065 | `[playful]` | 1,380 | `[humming]` | 346 | | `[excited]` | 3,980 | `[gasping]` | 1,266 | `[coughing]` | 333 | | `[sighing]` | 3,738 | `[scoffing]` | 1,010 | `[panting]` | 248 | | | | `[sad]` | 894 | `[voice breaking]` | 144 | | | | `[softly]` | 887 | `[singing]` | 95 | Rare tags (`[singing]`, `[yawning]` 59, `[sniffling]` 46) have too few examples to be reliable. Tag control is still weak in early checkpoints and strengthens as pre-training continues. ## Model architecture | Component | Details | |---|---| | Backbone | OmniVoice / Qwen3-0.6B, 28 layers, d = 1024. Bidirectional attention within a block, block-causal across blocks; earlier blocks are seen with all 10 codebooks | | Acoustic decoder | Axial MTP, 110M parameters: 6 layers over a (frame × codebook) grid, each with attention across the codebooks of a frame (causal) and across the frames of a codebook (the prompt, earlier blocks and the current block) | | Total parameters | ~0.75B (codec excluded) | | Audio codec | Fish Audio Drama 3 / S2 codec, 44.1 kHz, 21.5 frames/s, 1 semantic codebook (4096) + 9 residual codebooks (1024) | | Block size | 16 frames (0.74 s) | | Decoding | 6 confidence-ordered unmasking iterations per block with classifier-free guidance, then 9 axial-MTP steps (one per residual codebook); KV cache | | Length | predicted by the model (end-of-speech token) | ## Usage Requires the [code from GitHub](https://github.com/FashionFlora/ogg-tts), the OmniVoice weights (`k2-fsa/OmniVoice`) and the Fish Audio codec (`codec.pth` from `fishaudio/drama-3`). ```bash git clone https://github.com/FashionFlora/ogg-tts && cd ogg-tts git clone https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech ogg_tts/fish-speech export OMNIVOICE_PATH=$(huggingface-cli download k2-fsa/OmniVoice) export FISH_CODEC_PATH=$(huggingface-cli download fishaudio/drama-3 codec.pth) ``` ```python import sys sys.path.insert(0, "ogg_tts") from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download import infer_omnifish as inf, fish_codec as fc model, tok = inf.load_model(hf_hub_download("FashionFlora/ogg-tts", "model.safetensors"), "cuda") codec = fc.load_codec("cuda") codes = inf.generate_cached(model, tok, None, "", "[sighing] Hello! I am OGG, a text to speech model.", "en", cfg=1.5) audio = fc.decode(codec, codes[None].cuda())[0].float().cpu().numpy() # 44.1 kHz ``` **Voice cloning:** pass the reference audio's codes (`fc.encode`) and its exact transcript: ```python ref, _ = fc.encode(codec, wav_44k[None].cuda()) # wav_44k: torch tensor, mono, 44.1 kHz, up to ~15 s codes = inf.generate_cached(model, tok, ref[0].cpu(), "Transcript of the reference.", "Text to speak.", "en", cfg=1.5) ``` **Context:** neighbouring lines (not spoken) set the delivery, e.g. for a line of dialogue or the next sentence of a story: ```python codes = inf.generate_cached(model, tok, ref[0].cpu(), ref_text, "[frustrated] I told you already. I was at work.", "en", semantic_left=("Where were you last night?",), after=("At three in the morning?",), cfg=1.5) ``` **Guidance and pace.** `cfg` (classifier-free guidance) also sets the tempo: 1–1.5 gives the natural pace of the voice, 2 or more speaks faster and more pointedly. ## Training data About **8,200 hours** of studio-quality speech. The data is a private collection and is not publicly available. | Language | Hours | |---|---| | English | ~2,610 | | Polish | ~1,300 | | Spanish | ~820 | | German | ~750 | | Russian | ~645 | | French | ~500 | | Portuguese | ~300 | | Italian | ~290 | ## Training | | | |---|---| | Hardware | 1× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB) | | Schedule | 400k steps, 16k tokens per step, AdamW, cosine decay, bf16 | ### Compute and cost All training ran on a single rented AWS instance with **1× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB)** at **$3.36 per hour**. The figures below cover the whole rental, including setup, data processing and evaluation, not only the GPU time of the final model. Hours come from the run logs' timestamps and are approximate (±1 h per phase). #### GPU time | Phase | Period (UTC, 2026) | GPU hours | Cost (USD) | |---|---|---:|---:| | Setup: pilot runs, first OmniFish (NAR) run, audio tokenization, speaker embeddings | Oct 28 – Oct 30 | ~40 | ~$134 | | Baseline: OmniFish-BD with semantic left context (136k steps) | Oct 30 – Nov 1 | ~57 | ~$192 | | Ablations: context layouts, curricula, speaker modes, endpoint heads, MTP variants (v2–v25), axial-decoder smoke test | Nov 1 – Nov 3 | ~49 | ~$164 | | Fork A vs. fork B (axial decoder, prompt handling) | Nov 3 – Nov 4 | ~2.6 | ~$9 | | **Final model: OmniFish v26 (axial MTP decoder), 400k steps** | Nov 4 – ~Nov 11 | ~183 | ~$615 | | **Total** | | **~332** | **~$1,115** | The final run trains at about 2,200–2,500 steps per hour, about 100–110× real time in audio seen per hour. The ablations and the baseline account for **~$365, about one third** of the total. The final run is about half. #### Annotation (Gemini) Emotion and style tags and transcript checks were produced with Gemini Flash. | | Tokens | Rate (USD per 1M) | Cost (USD) | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Input | 294.8M | $0.50–1.00 | ~$220–295 | | Output | 87.3M | $3.00 | ~$262 | | **Total** | **382.1M** | | **~$480–560** | Rates follow the published Gemini 3 Flash list prices. Requests went through a third-party gateway, so the amounts actually billed may differ. Another 8.9M tokens went to a fallback model and are not priced here. #### Storage Amazon S3 (us-east-2), about 1.18 TB: **~$27 per month**. Upload and same-region transfer to training machines cost nothing. #### Summary | | Cost (USD) | |---|---:| | GPU (whole rental, including ablations) | ~$1,115 | | Annotation (Gemini) | ~$480–560 | | Storage (S3) | ~$27 / month | | **Total, one-off** | **~$1,595–1,675** | The total does not include the later Audio8 fine-tune, the stage-3 experiments on a second machine, or the cost of collecting the raw data. ## Evaluation Checkpoint 120k, `cfg=1.5`, one sample per item, no cherry-picking. WER with Whisper large-v3-turbo (tags removed from the reference), speaker similarity with ECAPA2 (cosine), pitch variation as the standard deviation of F0 in semitones. **Held-out recordings** (validation set: recordings and texts never trained on, 136 items in English, Spanish and German; a voice may also appear elsewhere in training). Each item clones the voice from a 6–10 s prompt and speaks two consecutive sentences that also exist as a real recording. The real recording, passed through the same codec, is the reference. | | OGG TTS 120k | Real recording | |---|---:|---:| | WER | **1.4 %** | 2.6 % | | Speaker similarity to the prompt | **0.773** | 0.737 | | Duration vs. the real recording (median) | 0.99 | 1.00 | | Pitch variation (F0 std, semitones) | 3.58 | 4.25 | | Language | Items | WER | Similarity to prompt | Duration ratio | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | English | 54 | 1.8 % | 0.777 | 0.98 | | Spanish | 78 | 1.2 % | 0.765 | 0.99 | | German | 4 | 0.6 % | 0.887 | 0.97 | **All 8 languages** (new texts, 32 items: a neutral and an angry line per voice, voices from the training set): WER 0.8 % on average, speaker similarity 0.785. | | EN | PL | ES | DE | RU | FR | PT | IT | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | WER | 0.0 % | 0.8 % | 0.0 % | 0.0 % | 0.0 % | 0.0 % | 3.3 % | 6.7 % | | Similarity | 0.780 | 0.767 | 0.828 | 0.824 | 0.763 | 0.708 | 0.771 | 0.841 | The tempo now matches real speech (duration ratio 0.99). Intonation is still about 15 % flatter than in the real recordings. Public benchmarks (Seed-TTS, CV3) follow with the final checkpoint. ## Limitations - Preview checkpoint: speaker similarity is not yet final, and the model may still mispronounce rare names. - Italian and Portuguese have the least training data. - Rare tags are not reliable yet. - Intonation is somewhat flatter than in real speech; `cfg` above 2 speeds the speech up. - Multi-speaker scenes in one pass are not part of this run; generate a dialogue line by line with context. ## License and responsible use - **Fish Audio codec.** The model generates Fish Audio codec tokens and needs the Fish Audio codec to produce audio. Use is subject to the [Fish Audio Community License](https://huggingface.co/FashionFlora/ogg-tts/blob/main/LICENSE-FISH-AUDIO.md) (see `NOTICE`). - **Real voices.** Do not use OGG TTS to imitate the voice of a real person without their consent, to impersonate, deceive, defraud or harass anyone, or to create sexual content involving minors. - **Research use.** The weights are released for research. ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{oggtts2026, title = {OGG TTS: Expressive Multilingual Text-to-Speech with Block Diffusion}, author = {FashionFlora}, year = {2026}, url = {https://huggingface.co/FashionFlora/ogg-tts} } ```

# DuplexJev-32B-Para (v1.5)

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev) · Release notes: [hearing the whole clip (v1.5)](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-11-full-length.md) · [Japanese as a third language](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-japanese.md) · [weak languages](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-weak-languages.md) · Research notes: [hearing stress](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-stress-understanding.md) · [keeping a speech-decision LLM able to talk](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-chat-replay.md)

🗣️ **Now with a voice:** DuplexJev-32B-Para is the ears of [Sophon-Realtime v1](https://github.com/adventists-ai/sophon-realtime), our open full-duplex voice model that hears your tone and speaks with one (open source on Nov 9, 2026).

**The DuplexJev model that hears the most beyond the words.** On top of everything
[DuplexJev-32B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Turn) and
[DuplexJev-32B-Stress](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Stress) do (spoken QA, gender, emotion,
turn-taking, stress and pauses), it also hears **laughter, breathing, coughs and sighs**, notices **how** someone is
talking (whispering, shouting, very fast or slow), and can tell, roughly as a person would, **whether two clips are
the same speaker**. Mandarin and English. Since v1.1 it also **holds a normal conversation**, multi-turn included.
**v1.2** adds **accent judgments** (English accents and Mandarin dialect regions) and much sharper **end-of-turn
detection right after the user pauses**: on LiveKit's eot-bench it now beats Smart Turn v3.2 in English and Chinese.
**v1.3** hears **stress** much better: on the public StressTest benchmark it goes from 72 to **85**, on StressPresso's
meaning questions from 69 to **89**, and on choosing the meaning a stressed word implies (DEBATE, held-out) from 85 to **93**, with the
other decisions about the same.
**v1.4** understands far more languages: **Japanese** error goes from 33 % to **12 %** (FLEURS) and from 38 % to
**11 %** on conversational Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese error falls to a quarter to a third of v1.3, Thai,
Arabic and Russian error by 30–40 %, and Mandarin conversational paralinguistics (laughter, breath, drawl, stutter …) are much sharper.
**v1.5** hears the **whole clip**: earlier versions (like every Qwen3-ASR-based checkpoint we trained) dropped the
last ~4 % of every 30 s audio chunk, because the connector assumed 6.25 audio tokens per second while the encoder
emits 6.5. v1.5 is retrained on the true length, which sharpens the decisions that depend on the end of an utterance:
**end-of-turn** (Smart Turn test set 93.3 → **94.4**, Chinese 91.4 → **94.6**; LiveKit eot-bench English false
cut-offs at 300 ms 20.4 → **17.7 %**), **stress** (StressTest 81.7 → **85.3**), and **emotion** in natural speech
(LISTEN emotion 32.4 → **33.2**, LISTEN non-verbal 48.8 → **51.6**), with spoken QA up a point as well.

> **v1.5 (2026-11-03)** replaces v1.4 (2026-10-22): audio is read at its true length (`"audio_full_length": true`
> in `config.json`). **Use `duplexjev-vllm>=0.4` / `duplexjev>=0.7`**, which read this flag; older versions still
> load the model but cut the last ~4 % of each 30 s chunk, as before.
> Earlier versions stay available as revisions `v1.4`, `v1.3`, `v1.2`, `v1.1` and `v1.0` (`--revision v1.4` in vLLM,
> `revision="v1.4"` in `from_pretrained`).

DuplexJev reads typed, closed-set decisions from speech as a **single-token distribution** of the LLM: zero decode
steps, many questions about the same clip in parallel. This repository is the complete model (Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder
+ connector + the language model of Qwen3-VL-32B, 33.0 B parameters, bf16; one 80 GB GPU).

**Which 32B to pick.** This one, for everything above.

## What changed

Starting from DuplexJev-32B-Turn we trained the connector and a new rank-16 LoRA on the LLM (merged here) for 4,000
steps. The mix is the 32B-Turn mix plus:

| added data | what it teaches |
|---|---|
| stress / pause detection (as in 32B-Stress: DEBATE, Stress-17K, TinyStress-15K, Expresso, neutral negatives) | which word is stressed, or none; where the pause is |
| speaker pairs (VoxCeleb1 dev, AISHELL-1, LibriSpeech, two-speaker mixtures) | same speaker or not; is this person in the clip |
| non-verbal sounds (VocalSound, NonVerbalSpeech-38K, NonverbalTTS, Expresso laughing) | is there laughter / breathing / a cough / a sigh / sniffing / throat clearing / a sneeze / crying …; negatives are cut from the same recordings away from the event |
| speaking style (EARS, Expresso whisper) | whispering, loud, fast, slow, high or low pitch, normal |
| spoken multiple-choice replay (ARC, OpenBookQA and CommonsenseQA train splits read by TTS) | keeps "answer the content" from being crowded out by "listen to the voice" |
| **v1.1:** conversation replay (spoken and typed user turns, up to 6 earlier turns as history; target = the original LLM's own reply) and in-house chat items | normal, full-length replies; trained with per-row loss averaging so long replies do not swamp the one-token decisions |
| **v1.2:** accents (VCTK, English Dialects, EdAcc, Common Voice accent labels, KeSpeech; held-out speakers kept for testing) | which accent: 19 English accents and 9 Mandarin dialect regions; native speaker or not; standard Mandarin or not; which English region |
| **v1.2:** end of turn right after a pause (otoSpeech-141h cut 0.2 s into each pause, with DualTurn labels; Smart Turn v3.2 training set) | finished vs. still talking / hesitating when the user has just gone quiet, the way a live voice agent has to decide |
| **v1.3:** the stress data re-balanced (more "which meaning does this stress imply" items, weight raised) and the gender data weighted ×2; no new corpora | choosing the meaning a stressed word implies; keeping gender where it was |
| **v1.4:** weak-language speech (ja, ko, vi, th, ar, ru: Emilia, Emilia-YODAS, YODAS2, Zeroth-Korean, VIVOS, FLEURS train, Common Voice; 162 k, labels re-checked with Qwen3-ASR-0.6B) + continuation (36 k) | transcribe and understand these languages |
| **v1.4:** Japanese speech (Emilia JA, Emilia-YODAS JA, Common Voice ja and other Japanese speech data; 358 k, re-checked) + Japanese continuation (20 k) | Japanese close to Chinese and English |
| **v1.4:** Mandarin conversational paralinguistics (licensed MagicData corpus, training speakers only; 42 k questions) | laughter, laughing while talking, breath, lip smack, sniff, cough, stressed word, drawl, which character is drawn out, stutter, sudden noise, unnatural pause, sentence emotion |
| **v1.4:** more emotion classes (surprise, fear, anxiety, excitement, encouragement, apologetic, playful) from CSEMOTIONS, EmotionTalk, DailyTalk, JL-Corpus, EMNS, Emozionalmente, SUBESCO | emotions beyond the basic four |
| **v1.5:** the whole v1.4 mix again, now with audio tokens at the encoder's true length (6.5 per second); transcription items with native-language instructions and leading / trailing silence (FLEURS dev split, the v1.4 weak-language speech); a light replay of all emotion data | the end of every clip is heard; always transcribe when asked to; emotion kept sharp |

v1.4 was trained from v1.3 in four short stages (2,000 + 2,000 + 1,500 + 1,000 steps; connector + a new rank-16 LoRA
each time, merged here), replaying the full v1.3 mix in every stage; the last two stages raise the stress,
non-verbal, emotion and speaking-style replay ×1.5 each.

v1.5 was trained from v1.4 in two stages (2,000 + 1,500 steps; connector + a new rank-16 LoRA each time, merged
here) with the audio-token count computed from the encoder's real output length.

## v1.5 vs v1.4

| | v1.4 | **v1.5** |
|---|---:|---:|
| qa100 / ZJU-ML (vLLM, client wording) | 97 / 90 | **98 / 91** |
| gender / emotion (vLLM) | 92.1 / 89.2 | **92.6 / 90.0** |
| Easy-Turn* (vLLM) | 94.1 | **95.4** |
| Smart Turn v3.2 test set, all / Chinese (threshold 0.5) | 93.3 / 91.4 | **94.4 / 94.6** |
| eot-bench, English false cut-offs at 300 / 600 ms (with the assistant's previous message, fast mode) | 20.4 / 8.9% | **17.7 / 7.0%** |
| eot-bench, Chinese, same setting | 42.3 / 13.8% | **41.0 / 13.3%** |
| StressTest / StressPresso (which meaning the stress implies) | 81.7 / 88.6 | **85.3 / 89.1** |
| DEBATE: stressed word / pause position | 89.8 / 79.8 | **90.7 / 81.4** |
| LISTEN (EACL 2026) emotion / non-verbal, audio only | 32.4 / 48.8 | **33.2 / 51.6** |
| EmotionTalk / CSEMOTIONS emotion (test splits)† | 62.6 / 89.8 | **68.5 / 94.2** |

Same harness for both columns (stress, LISTEN and emotion rows: single-token readout, PyTorch, % correct).
† In-domain: the training splits of these corpora are in the replay data.

## v1.4 vs v1.3

Languages (FLEURS test, 150 utterances per language, median word / character error, lower is better):

| | ja | ko | vi | th | ar | ru | zh | en | es | fr | de |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| v1.3 | 32.7 | 31.8 | 41.7 | 29.1 | 27.0 | 10.6 | 3.8 | 1.5 | 4.4 | 8.5 | 5.3 |
| **v1.4** | **11.6** | **7.6** | **14.6** | **18.0** | **19.4** | **6.9** | 3.8 | 0.0 | 3.5 | 7.0 | 5.3 |
| encoder ceiling (Qwen3-ASR-0.6B) | 7.0 | 2.7 | 7.8 | 5.1 | 16.7 | 7.8 | 2.0 | 1.3 | 3.4 | 6.2 | 5.6 |

Japanese, conversational (held-out Emilia JA shard) / Common Voice ja test, character error: v1.3 38.2 / 33.3 →
**v1.4 11.1 / 13.0** (encoder 8.3 / 10.8).

Mandarin conversational paralinguistics (licensed MagicData corpus, held-out speakers, accuracy %; yes/no unless noted):

| | breath | lip smack | laughter | laughing while talking | sniff | cough | drawl | stressed word (4-way) | emotion (4-way) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **v1.4** | 91.7 | 85.8 | 89.3 | 87.8 | 87.5 | 71.4 | 79.4 | 85.3 | 70.7 |

(v1.3 was not trained on this corpus; the 4B-Para v1.1, also untrained on it, scores 50–66 on the yes/no rows.)

Accent, same-speaker and turn-taking (eot-bench, Smart Turn) were **not re-run** for v1.4; the numbers in the next
sections are v1.3's.

## Results (v1.3 and earlier)

| | 32B-Turn | 32B-Para v1.1 | 32B-Para v1.2 | **32B-Para v1.3** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| qa100 / ZJU-ML | 96 / 87 | 96 / 88 | 95 / 87 | 96 / 87 |
| gender / emotion | 91.5 / 91.1 | 92.9 / 91.5 | 93.9 / 90.1 | 93.8 / 92.1 |
| VoiceBench OBQA‡ / MMSU | 85.5 / 72.1 | 94.5 / 75.5 | 94.3 / 75.0 | 94.1 / 75.7 |
| Easy-Turn* | 95.2 | 94.8 | **95.5** | 94.4 |
| which word is stressed, "none" offered: DEBATE (zh) / StressPresso (en) | 35 / 1 | 93 / 96 | 92 / 91 | **95 / 96** |
| neutral speech → "no word is stressed": AISHELL-1 / LibriSpeech | 92 / 50 | 100 / 99 | 99 / — | 98 / 83 |
| **meaning from stress: DEBATE held-out / StressTest** | 35 / 52 | 85 / 76 | 85 / 72 | **93 / 85** |
| StressPresso, which meaning the stress implies (English) | — | — | 69 | **89** |
| **laughter / breathing / cough / sigh** (AUC, NonverbalTTS test, real speech, unseen) | — | 0.88 / 0.81 / 0.85 / 0.80 | 0.87 / 0.81 / 0.84 / 0.75 | ≈ v1.2† |
| laughter / breathing in natural Mandarin conversation (AUC, unseen third-party sample) | — | 0.83 / 0.65 | 0.80 / 0.56 | ≈ v1.2† |
| **speaking style, 7 classes** (EARS held-out speakers) | — | 82% | 79% | 80% |
| same speaker? EER, VoxCeleb1 random / hard pairs (our harness) | — | 28.2% / 39.6% | 31.2% / 42.3% | 29.1% / 38.4%◊ |

Through vLLM with `duplexjev-vllm` in the client wording, v1.3: qa100 97, ZJU-ML 90, gender 92.1, emotion 91.8,
Easy-Turn 94.5 (v1.2: 98, 90, 93.6, 89.8, 95.5; v1.1: 97, 91, 93.2, 90.0, 94.8; qa100 and ZJU-ML have 100 items each).
"—": not re-run for that version.

- † v1.3 non-verbal sounds were checked by accuracy on the same test sets (NonverbalTTS, NonVerbalSpeech-38K,
  VocalSound, Expresso, MagicData): within a few points of v1.2 either way; AUC not re-run.
- ◊ Same harness re-run for v1.2: 30.7% / 38.2% (the v1.2 column is from an earlier run).

  human-like sense of "same voice or not", not to identify people.

## Turn-taking benchmarks (v1.2 / v1.3; v1.5 in the table above)

**LiveKit [eot-bench](https://github.com/livekit/eot-bench)** (validation set, decision 0.2 s into each pause, official
metrics). False cut-offs when the agent may wait at most 300 / 600 ms (lower is better):

| | English | Chinese |
|---|---:|---:|
| LiveKit Turn Detector v1 | 9.9 / 4.5% | 20.6 / 8.7% |
| **DuplexJev-32B-Para v1.2, with the assistant's previous message** (plugin default, full eot-bench run) | **20.0 / 9.4%** | **37.7 / 12.2%** |
| DuplexJev-32B-Para v1.2, with the assistant's previous message, `readout="act"` (fast mode) | 18.4 / 7.9% | 37.3 / 12.3% |
| DuplexJev-32B-Para v1.2, audio only (fast mode) | 23.5 / 11.1% | 40.0 / 12.8% |
| **DuplexJev-32B-Para v1.3, with the assistant's previous message** (fast mode) | 20.3 / 8.8% | **35.5** / 12.3% |
| DuplexJev-32B-Para v1.3, audio only (fast mode) | 24.7 / 11.2% | 38.8 / 12.0% |
| DuplexJev-32B-Turn, audio only (fast mode) | 29.8 / 13.9% | 44.9 / 14.5% |
| Smart Turn v3.2 | 35.2 / 14.8% | 42.9 / 13.2% |

eot-bench audio is not in our training data. "With the assistant's previous message" puts
`The assistant had just said: "..."` before the audio; the Pipecat and LiveKit plugins send it
(`pipecat-duplexjev>=0.3`, `livekit-plugins-duplexjev>=0.2`, gateway `duplexjev>=0.6`). Plugin default: the turn
question, P(finished) + P(backchannel); run with every eot-bench decision point (adapter
`benchmarks/turn_detection/eot_bench/duplexjev_ctx_adapter.py` on GitHub). `readout="act"` (`pipecat-duplexjev>=0.4`,
`livekit-plugins-duplexjev>=0.3`): question "What should the assistant do now?", P(reply now) + P(short
acknowledgement). Rows marked fast mode ask once per pause, at the 0.2 s score point.

**Pipecat [Smart Turn v3.2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/pipecat-ai/smart-turn-data-v3.2-test) test set**
(accuracy at threshold 0.5): v1.2 English 94.0% (Smart Turn v3.2: 94.7%), Chinese 91.1% (90.5%); v1.3 94.2% / 91.4%; DuplexJev-32B-Turn
65.2% / 84.6%. The Smart Turn v3.2 *training* set is in our training mix, so this is an in-distribution result.

## Serve with vLLM

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" "duplexjev-vllm>=0.4"
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Para --max-model-len 4096
```

`duplexjev-vllm>=0.4` reads `"audio_full_length": true` from `config.json` and feeds the whole clip; `DJ_FULL_LEN=0`
forces the old truncated length, `DJ_FULL_LEN=1` the full length for any checkpoint.

Prompt format and client are the same as for [DuplexJev-32B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Turn);
see [`examples/vllm_client.py`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/examples/vllm_client.py). Examples:

```
The user said: <|audio|>

Is there laughter in this audio?

Options:
A. Yes
B. No

Answer with the letter only.
```

```
用户说：<|audio|>

除了说话，这段音频里还有哪种声音？

选项：
A. 叹气
B. 咳嗽
C. 笑声
D. 都没有

请只回答选项字母。
```

Always offer a "none" option for stress and non-verbal questions; the model was trained with it.

## Limitations

- Accent and same-speaker scores were not re-measured for v1.4 / v1.5.
- Thai and Arabic are still 2–3× the encoder's own error.
- Non-verbal training audio is mostly acted (radio drama, animation, studio recordings); in natural conversation the
  scores are lower (see the table).
- Breathing in natural Mandarin conversation is weak (AUC 0.56 in v1.2, 0.65 in v1.1, 0.78 in v1.0); acted / read
  speech is much better.
- Accent answers describe how someone sounds, not where they are from or who they are; accents are often mixed or
  ambiguous. Do not use them to make decisions about people.
- Asked about itself, it may describe abilities (seeing images, speaking) that this checkpoint does not have on its
  own: it takes speech and text and replies in text.
- Speaker judgments are coarse (EER 18–40%) and must not be used to identify or verify people.
- Emotion labels come from acted corpora; do not use the outputs to make decisions about individuals.

# Africa TTS

**Africa TTS** is a [Pocket TTS](https://github.com/kyutai-labs/pocket-tts) text-to-speech model for **92 African languages and English**, with voice cloning from a few seconds of audio. Text is read as IPA, produced by [africa-g2p](https://github.com/AfriSpeech/africa-g2p). This is the 24-layer model; [Africa TTS Turbo](https://huggingface.co/AfriSpeech/africa-tts-turbo) is its fast 6-layer distilled version.

🎙️ **Try it live:** [type text, hear it spoken](https://huggingface.co/spaces/AfriSpeech/africa-tts-demo) (Turbo, 93 trained + 657 experimental languages, own-voice cloning).

🔊 **Listen:** [samples in every language](https://huggingface.co/spaces/AfriSpeech/africa-tts-samples) — Articles 1, 3 and 5 of the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights, read in 53 languages.

## Quick start

Code, training recipe and mobile deployment: **[github.com/AfriSpeech/africa-tts](https://github.com/AfriSpeech/africa-tts)**.

```bash
pip install "africa-tts @ git+https://github.com/AfriSpeech/africa-tts"
# English also needs espeak-ng: apt install espeak-ng / brew install espeak-ng
africa-tts "Akwaaba! Yɛfrɛ me Kofi." --lang twi --model africa-tts -o out.wav
```

```python
from africa_tts import AfricaTTS

tts = AfricaTTS.load("africa-tts")
audio = tts.generate("Akwaaba! Yɛfrɛ me Kofi.", lang="twi")              # default Twi voice
audio = tts.generate("Hello Ghana!", lang="eng", voice="my_voice.wav")  # clone any 3-10 s clip
tts.save(audio, "out.wav")
```

- **Default voices:** every language has one, 3.5-6 s of real speech in that language: a female
  voice from [africa-female-speech-v2-best60](https://huggingface.co/datasets/AfriSpeech/africa-female-speech-v2-best60)
  (highest-rated clip) for the 17 languages it covers (Amharic, Chichewa, Hausa, Igbo,
  Kinyarwanda, Rundi, Sepedi, Shona, Swahili, Swati, Tigrinya, Tsonga, Twi, Venda, Xhosa, Yoruba,
  Zulu), a JW recording for the others (English: Ghanaian English), in
  [voices/](https://huggingface.co/AfriSpeech/africa-tts/tree/main/voices).
- **Numbers:** spell them out. Every training clip with a numeral was removed.
- **On device:** a [sherpa-onnx](https://github.com/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx) bundle of this model (unguided) is in [sherpa-onnx/](https://huggingface.co/AfriSpeech/africa-tts/tree/main/sherpa-onnx) (ONNX models, G2P tables, default voices, English espeak-ng data); see the [mobile guide](https://github.com/AfriSpeech/africa-tts/tree/main/mobile).
- **API server:** a Docker HTTP/WebSocket server (OpenAI-compatible endpoint included) on
  sherpa-onnx, CPU only: see [server/](https://github.com/AfriSpeech/africa-tts/tree/main/server).
- **Two modes:** *guided* (classifier-free guidance 2.0, used when you load this model with the `africa-tts` package: two backbone passes per frame, Python only) and *unguided* (`cfg=1.0`: one pass per frame, also on device via sherpa-onnx). A third option is [Africa TTS Turbo](https://huggingface.co/AfriSpeech/africa-tts-turbo): 6 layers with guidance distilled in. Which suits you best can depend on the language: listen to the samples and try them.

### Without the package

Plain pocket-tts works too and runs the model unguided (pocket-tts has no guidance). The model reads **IPA**, not spelling, so text must be
converted exactly as in training. Use
africa-g2p at commit `76b53a8`: the 0.3.2 release on PyPI predates fixes to the Ghanaian tables
and gives different IPA for Twi, Fante, Ewe, Igbo and Rundi.

```python
# pip install "pocket-tts>=4.0.1" "africa-g2p[english] @ git+https://github.com/AfriSpeech/africa-g2p@76b53a8"
import re
import scipy.io.wavfile
from africa_g2p import g2p
from pocket_tts import TTSModel

_PUNCT = re.compile(r"^(\W*)(.*?)(\W*)$", re.S)

def to_ipa(text: str, lang: str) -> str:
    """Text -> the IPA the model was trained on. lang: ISO 639-3 code (see the table below)."""
    if lang != "eng":
        return g2p(text, lang, output="ipa")
    words = []  # English (espeak-ng): word by word, keeping punctuation, as in training
    for w in text.split():
        lead, core, trail = _PUNCT.match(w).groups()
        words.append(lead + (g2p(core, "eng", output="ipa").replace(" ", "") if core else "") + trail)
    return " ".join(words)

model = TTSModel.load_model(config="hf://AfriSpeech/africa-tts/config.yaml")
voice = model.get_state_for_audio_prompt("hf://AfriSpeech/africa-tts/voices/twi.wav")
audio = model.generate_audio(voice, to_ipa("Akwaaba! Yɛfrɛ me Kofi.", "twi"))
scipy.io.wavfile.write("out.wav", model.sample_rate, audio.numpy())
```

The config turns off Pocket TTS's first-letter capitalisation and character replacement, since
the input is IPA.

## Model

24-layer FlowLM (d_model 1024, 316M parameters) + Mimi codec (24 kHz, 12.5 Hz frames). Kyutai's new-language recipe (`finetune_language`): warm start from Kyutai's English 24-layer model (`english_2026-04_24l`) with a fresh text table for a new 4,000-token IPA SentencePiece (Unigram) tokenizer; nothing frozen; lr 2e-4 constant after 1k warmup; batch 64; LSD flow; text and voice dropout 0.2; EMA 0.999. Validated every 1k steps, early-stopped at 113k (best validation loss at 93k). The released weights are the **100k** checkpoint (EMA), chosen by listening.

## Training data

897 hours of real speech (no synthetic or voice-converted audio):

| Source | Hours | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| JW recordings via [AfriSpeech Selector](https://github.com/AfriSpeech/afrispeech-selector) | 383 | read speech, `afrispeech` (JW) source only; native sample rate |
| [AfriSpeech/africa-female-speech-v2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/AfriSpeech/africa-female-speech-v2) | 192 | 24 kHz, Demucs-cleaned |
| Ghanaian English | 156 | |
| [HiFiTTS-2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/hifitts-2) (English) | 166 | 200 h slice, training only |

Processing:
- Clips of 1-30 s; **any clip whose transcript contains a number was dropped** (digits and other
  numerals such as Ge'ez).
- Word timings from [ctc-forced-aligner](https://github.com/MahmoudAshraf97/ctc-forced-aligner)
  (`MahmoudAshraf/mms-300m-1130-forced-aligner`, uroman romanisation) for every language; 99.95% of
  clips aligned. Voice prompts are the start of the same clip, cut at a word boundary.
- Words converted to IPA with africa-g2p's C library (the same tables as the Python package);
  English with espeak-ng (en-us) plus africa-g2p's normalisation. Only languages with an africa-g2p
  IPA table were kept.

## Limitations

- **Mostly read religious speech.** Most African-language hours are JW readings, so news,
  conversation and technical vocabulary are less natural; low-hour languages (under ~2 h) are weak.
- **Tone:** some africa-g2p tables do not mark tone (e.g. Fon, Ewe, Igbo, Ga), so the model has to
  guess it from context.
- **Loanwords** are converted with the host language's spelling rules ("Japanese" in Twi becomes
  `d͡ʒapanese`).
- No numerals (see above). No language tag: the language comes from the IPA and the voice prompt.
- Voice cloning can reproduce anyone's voice. Do not use it to impersonate people or without consent.

# Drama 3 for ComfyUI — fp8 experts, bf16 dense

A conversion of **fishaudio/drama-3** for the [ComfyUI-Drama3](https://github.com/PedroMarinhoDev/ComfyUI-Drama3) node pack.

- **Copied from:** <https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3> — revision `78e5ab79e49a`, the weights uploaded **2026-10-29** (15 shards; the earlier 8-shard files were removed upstream that day).
- **Script used:** `tools/convert.py` from <https://github.com/PedroMarinhoDev/ComfyUI-Drama3>
  `python tools/convert.py model <drama-3 folder> drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors --format fp8`
- **What is in the file:** the routed experts are the checkpoint's own block-FP8 tensors (128x128 scales) copied byte for byte; every other linear keeps the checkpoint's bf16. Gate/up projections are fused; the LM head is trimmed to the rows generation samples from (1 end-of-speech + 4096 semantic tokens).
- **How to use:** put the file in `ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models/` and load it with the `Drama3Loader` node. Pair it with `drama3_codec.safetensors` in `ComfyUI/models/vae/` and Qwen3-ASR in `ComfyUI/models/asr/` (both from the pack's own Hub repos).
- **File:** `drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors` — 38,578,417,928 bytes, 912 tensors, sha256 `cfd27b526b35a66729ffd1d6966bf13f7856f4c59f917497eaded6ecb0b888de`.

Note: the prebuilt file in `PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI` comes from an **earlier revision** of the base model. This file matches the 2026-10-29 weights, and its tensors were verified byte-identical to that checkpoint.
